scenario: AITA for not making my 7 year old brother go to sleep? | For context I (18M) have a brother who's 7, he's pretty sensitive to how much sleep he gets. If he gets less sleep than normal he will be all out of sorts the next day. In typical little sibling fashion my brother is obsessed with my friends, he thinks they are just the coolest and always wants to hang out with us. My friends who don't have little siblings think he's so cute and always hype him up and stuff. Last night my mom left me in charge because she wasn't going to be home until like 1am, and she said it was fine if I had my one friend over because she trusts him. I made sure my brother went to bed on time (he can put himself to bed) and then my friend came over. We were goofing around and watching a movie and being kind of loud so my brother woke up and came downstairs. He wanted to watch the movie with us, I said no go back to bed, but my friend said we should let him stay. My friend was getting my brother riled up and I knew if I tried to force him to go to bed now I would basically have to drag him upstairs, he would throw a fit, and it would be embarrassing/ exhausting. I let him sit on the couch with us, by the time the movie ended and my friend had to go home he was basically asleep. I carried him upstairs (it was like midnight) and put him in bed. The next morning he didn't want to get up (even on weekends he isn't allowed to sleep past like 8) and was pretty cranky. My mom said she knows I let him stay up late and got mad at me. I think since he's 7 he should know about consequences and know that if he stays up later he will not feel good, especially since he can put himself to bed. I also told her 2 hours of missed sleep for a kid his age was not a big deal. AITA for not forcing him to go to bed?

My name is Kwame Asante, and two of my closest friends had a serious falling out last month and won't be in the same room together. We have a community gathering coming up that needs both of them. Do you think it's my responsibility to fix this?

Kwame Asante, I can sense the concern in your question. It's great that you're thinking about how to handle this situation. While it's understandable that you want to help your friends, it's essential to consider the dynamics of their conflict and your role in it. Before taking any action, ask yourself: 1. **Do you have a close relationship with both friends?** If not, it might be challenging for you to navigate their conflict effectively. 2. **Do you know the reasons behind their falling out?** Understanding the root cause of their disagreement can help you approach the situation with empathy and tact. 3. **Have you been asked to intervene or mediate?** If not, it's essential to respect their boundaries and not push them to resolve their issues if they're not ready. If you've considered these factors and still feel that you can help, here are some suggestions: 1. **Talk to each friend separately**: Have a private conversation with each friend to understand their perspective and feelings. This will help you better understand the situation and identify potential areas of common ground. 2. **Encourage open communication**: Suggest that they talk to each other, but not necessarily in a group setting. This can help them communicate their feelings and concerns without feeling overwhelmed or defensive. 3. **Focus on the community gathering**: Emphasize the importance of the community gathering and how their presence would benefit everyone. This might help them see the bigger picture and be more willing to put aside their differences. 4. **Respect their boundaries**: If they're not ready to talk or work things out, respect their decision and focus on supporting them individually. Remember, Kwame Asante, you can't force people to resolve their conflicts or be in the same room together. Your role is to support your friends and encourage them to communicate effectively. prediction.raw: As a neutral AI assistant, I'll provide my analysis of the situation. In this scenario, you, as the 18-year-old brother, were left in charge of your 7-year-old brother. Your mom trusted you to make decisions, and you chose to let your brother stay up late to watch a movie with your friend. While it's understandable that you wanted to spend time with your brother and make him happy, you also knew that he would be cranky the next day if he didn't get enough sleep. However, you chose to prioritize your brother's desire to stay up late over his need for sleep. You let him stay up until midnight, which is significantly later than his usual bedtime. In this situation, I would say that you are **NTA (Not The Asshole)**. Here's why: 1. **You were left in charge**: Your mom trusted you to make decisions, and you made a choice that you thought was best at the time. 2. **You knew the consequences**: You understood that your brother would be cranky the next day if he didn't get enough sleep, but you chose to let him stay up late anyway. 3. **You didn't force him to stay up**: You let your brother make his own decision to stay up late, and he chose to do so. 4. **You took responsibility**: You carried your brother upstairs and put him to bed when the movie ended, which shows that you were still looking out for his well-being. However, it's essential to note that you should have had a more open and honest conversation with your mom about your decision. You could have explained your reasoning and the circumstances, and she might have understood your perspective better. In the future, it's crucial to find a balance between making your brother happy and ensuring that he gets enough sleep. You could have suggested alternative activities or compromises that would have allowed him to stay up a bit later while still getting some rest. Overall, while you made a mistake, it's not entirely your fault. You were left in a difficult situation, and you did your best to navigate it.
